newsitem.title: USA: Hungary wins Western praise as others falter.
newsitem.headline: Hungary wins Western praise as others falter.

text.p: Hungary won praise from Western bankers and monetary sources on Thursday, even though some other emerging market economies are faltering on the way to growth and stability.

"The economy is doing pretty well," said one international monetary source. "The current account remains on target in respect to the (IMF) programme and inflation is perfectly on target, almost month by month."

An IMF delegation left Hungary last month after reviewing its economy. Finance Ministry sources said the IMF assessment had been positive, although the monitoring mission had been worried about a larger than expected social security deficit.
Hungary has IMF funds of about $365 million available to draw on, but has not used this money. The IMF board is due to review the situation in the autumn.

The monetary source said he did not expect Hungary to face the currency problems seen by fellow reformers in the Czech republic, which abandoned its fixed exchange rate in May, or by Thailand, which floated the baht this week.
"When there were problems in the Czech republic, there was nothing of the kind happening in Hungary," he said. "The forint remains within its exchange rate band."

The forint, currently trading at about 188 to the dollar, is fixed within a downward crawling basket of the dollar and the mark. It is currently allowed to decline by 1.1 percent a month, but the decline will ease to one percent from August.

The monetary sources said the financial impact of Hungary's likely membership of the Western NATO alliance was not clear, although it was encouraging that officials appeared to want to increase military spending only gradually.

"It is not clear what the implications of NATO membership are in terms of costs for the budget, but I do not think it is going to be dramatic," he said. "If there is an increase in spending, I think it is important that it is gradual."

Monetary officials have said they are worried about higher military spending in central Europe, although Romania, which is boosting arms spending amid a deep economic crisis, has faced more criticism than the three top NATO membership contenders -- Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
Hungary is forecasting three percent economic growth this year, after one percent last year, and analysts noted that Budapest was now catching up with its rival reformers.

"It's really the case of the tortoise and the hare -- they were the tortoise and the Czech Republic was the hare," said Charles Blitzer, chief economist, emerging markets at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
"Obviously things are going better than expected, growth has come back faster than people expected and the stock market is booming. But the economy is still not as strong as Poland."
Hungarian inflation is expected to fall to 13.5 percent in 1988, from 18 percent in 1987 and 23.6 percent last year.

"Maybe more could have been achieved on inflation in 1997, but because the target has been well within reach, the announcement for 1998 has become more credible," the monetary source said. "Even the unions seem to view it as credible."
